title: 5 scale trends Mistakes That Are Destroying Your weekly averages
description: Five scale mistakes corrupt the weekly average until it lies to you daily. Weigh through the test, audit your habits against the five, and restore the one instrument a gainer cannot afford to have broken.

scenes.narration: Today we audit the scale. | First, this week's weigh-ins. | However many you have. | Average what exists, honestly. | Note how many are missing. | That count matters too. | Second, max strict push-ups. | Floor to lockout, clean. | Count the honest reps. | That is your second number. | Ahead: five scale mistakes. | Count how many are yours. | Keep the pair together. | At the end I tell | you which mistake lies loudest. | The weekly average is your | finest instrument. | But instruments can be mishandled | into lying. | Most broken trends are broken | by handling, not by the | body. | Let us check your handling.

scenes.label: SCALE MISTAKES THAT CORRUPT THE AVERAGE
scenes.sub: 0 mistakes: the instrument reads true - 3 plus: your trend is fiction
scenes.narration: Here is the grading. Zero mistakes: your average is an honest instrument and every decision you have made from it stands on rock. One or two: the normal score, small leaks in the data that a week of discipline seals. Three or more: your trend is partly fiction, and any frustration you feel about your gaining must be re-examined, because you have been steering by a compass with a magnet taped to it. The mistakes are ordered by the damage they do to the number itself, and the first is the one that converts a precision instrument into a mood ring. Count honestly. A corrupted average is worse than no average, because it produces confident wrong decisions, the most expensive kind.

Mistake one: weighing at random times. Morning and evening weights differ by the day's food, water, and activity, often by more than a kilo, so an average built from mixed hours measures your schedule's chaos, not your tissue. Mistake two: reacting to single days, cutting food after a water spike or celebrating a drained morning, which injects your emotions into the data as steering inputs. Mistake three: the selective record, writing down the flattering mornings and forgetting the others, which biases the average downward or upward depending on your hopes and quietly falsifies the trend. The mechanism under all three is the same: the average is only as honest as the collection, and collection is a ritual before it is a statistic. Mistake three has a modern accomplice: the smart scale's app, which smooths, estimates, and body-fat-percentages your mornings into a dashboard of confident fiction. Use the scale's raw number and your own average. The app's extra metrics are entertainment wearing a lab coat, and entertainment is not an instrument.

Mistake four: changing the instrument mid-stream, a new scale, a new floor spot, carpet instead of tile, each silently shifting the readings by amounts larger than a week's real gain. Mistake five: demanding daily meaning, asking a slow instrument fast questions until the noise where an answer should be drives a good man to quit a working plan. The measurement science here is old and settled: consistency of conditions is what makes small changes detectable, and the detectable change in a week of gaining is a few hundred grams, smaller than every error on this list. That is the whole audit in one sentence. Your signal is small, so your handling must be exact, and exact handling is a set of habits, not a talent. One more piece of measurement science seals the audit: the floor itself is part of the instrument. A scale on carpet or a flexing board under-reads and wanders, because the surface absorbs force unevenly. Hard, flat, and permanent is the specification, which is why the protocol treats the spot as sacred.

The deep pattern under the five mistakes is that each one protects a feeling at the expense of a fact. Random times protect convenience. Daily reactions protect the feeling of control. Selective records protect hope. Instrument changes protect the story that the old scale was wrong. Daily meaning protects urgency. A scientist's relationship with an instrument is the opposite trade: he surrenders the feelings, convenience, control, hope, and urgency, in exchange for numbers that will still be true next year. That surrender is the actual skill this season has been teaching under all its topics. Protein counts, gap maps, surplus estimates, and averages are one skill wearing four costumes: preferring the true number to the kind one.

Your advantage in fixing these mistakes is that instrument repair is instant and total. A broken training habit takes months to rebuild. A broken weighing ritual is fixed tomorrow morning, completely, by deciding the hour, the spot, and the record, and the data becomes trustworthy within a fortnight. There is a second advantage: your trend, once honest, is a gentle signal to steer by, because your corrections are snack-sized. The dieter's corrupted average can cost him months of wrong restriction. Yours costs you a misjudged handful of nuts. Skinny guys live close to the truth in this game, small signals, small errors, small corrections, and the man who keeps his instruments clean in a small-signal world is nearly impossible to fool, including by himself.

Measure your effort the same honest way. Four rounds of push-ups, forty seconds on, twenty off. Same strict form every round, no generous counting. An instrument you cannot fool is what we are building, in the gym and on the scale alike.

The instrument protocol, four rules. One: fix the ritual, same scale, same hard floor spot, same moment after waking, before food and drink, written on a card beside the scale if memory needs help. Two: record every number the moment it appears, in one unbroken list, especially the ones you dislike, because disliked numbers are data with the highest information content. Three: compute the average every Sunday and file the week, rigged or clean, with a one-word note if it was rigged. Four: act only on the two-week signals and monthly reviews this season prescribes, in the small steps prescribed, so the instrument's readings are never again chased by a single morning's mood.

Your verdict, the pair read together. Zero mistakes and modest push-ups: your instrument is true and your engine is the project, a clean division of labor. One or two mistakes with any number: seal them this week and treat next month's trend as your first fully honest one, a small rebirth worth marking. Three or more mistakes: every past conclusion drawn from your scale is provisionally withdrawn, not in shame but in science, and the retest in thirty days begins your real record. A true instrument and climbing push-ups: you are running a laboratory, not a hope, and laboratories produce results on schedule. Comment your mistake count and your push-up number. The confession repairs the instrument faster than any purchase. If your count today was high, let the verdict be a beginning rather than an indictment. Every man in this audience has steered by a broken instrument at some point. The ones who gain are simply the ones who repaired it before blaming the road.

Thirty days from now, bring me four clean weekly averages and the same push-up test. Bring me an instrument that reads true and a bigger number. Subscribe, and let the ritual run unbroken until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
